query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of rare earth elements, specifically 1 wt% of Cerium (Ce), to boride-based components will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by 35% relative to the baseline of unmodified boride-based components, under the conditions of hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment operating at temperatures between 600°C to 700°C.
generation.intervention: Addition of 1 wt% of Cerium (Ce) to the boride-based components
generation.conditions: Hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment operating at temperatures between 600°C to 700°C
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide layer enriched with Cerium
generation.mechanism: The rare earth element Cerium reacts with oxygen to form a stable and dense oxide layer on the surface of the boride-based components, which acts as a barrier to prevent the penetration of molten aluminum and subsequent corrosion
generation.predicted_outcome: 35% improvement in resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion
generation.uncertainty: The actual improvement in corrosion resistance may vary depending on the specific processing conditions, the type of boride-based component, and the presence of other impurities or elements

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured corrosion rate of the modified boride-based components is not at least 25% lower than that of the unmodified components, the hypothesis is falsified

frame.system: boride-based components in contact with molten aluminum
prior_attempts: existing boride-based components without additional protection
